props.title: Full Frontal
props.initialSlug: A raw look at Hollywood lives over 24 crazy hours

sections.content: Full Frontal (2002) represents Steven Soderbergh's experimental dive into meta-filmmaking, arriving at the height of his mainstream success with Ocean's Eleven (2001). Shot on digital video with a skeleton crew, it's a deliberately messy examination of Hollywood's layers of artifice. The film shares DNA with Adaptation (2002) and Living in Oblivion (1995) in its self-reflexive exploration of moviemaking, but Soderbergh pushes further into raw territory by using handheld cameras and natural lighting to create a stark contrast with the film-within-a-film's glossy aesthetic.

sections.content: The film's structure deliberately disorients, jumping between multiple narrative threads and reality levels. Like Mulholland Drive (2001), it plays with audience expectations about what's "real" within its universe. Soderbergh's approach echoes the French New Wave's deconstruction of cinema, particularly Day for Night (1973), but with a distinctly digital-age sensibility. The improvisational feel and documentary-style footage anticipate later works like Inland Empire (2006).

The performances, particularly Julia Roberts playing dual roles, highlight the film's preoccupation with authenticity versus performance. This theme connects to other Hollywood self-examinations like The Player (1992) and State and Main (2000), but Full Frontal strips away the glossy satire for something more raw and uncomfortable. sections.content: Soderbergh's choice to shoot on early digital video wasn't just economic - it was prophetic. Like Timecode (2000) and Russian Ark (2002), Full Frontal pushed the boundaries of what digital filmmaking could achieve, paving the way for later digital innovators like Tangerine (2015) and Unsane (2018). The grainy, immediate quality of the footage creates an intentional contrast with traditional film, commenting on Hollywood's obsession with surface perfection.

The film's release timing is crucial - coming after Soderbergh's Oscar win for Traffic (2000) and commercial success with Erin Brockovich (2000), it reads as both an artistic rebellion and a meditation on success in Hollywood. Its experimental nature aligns with other director's "palate cleansers" like Schizopolis (1996) and Bubble (2005), where established filmmakers deliberately break from convention.
